keySentence: The best adventures start when you stop being bored.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: When Milo came home from his adventure he looked at everything around him with completely new eyes. His bedroom was the same but it seemed full of things worth noticing that he had never noticed before. His street had always been there but now he could see details in it that were genuinely interesting. He wondered how he had ever walked through the same world and found nothing worth paying attention to. The boredom had not been in the world — it had been entirely inside his own way of looking at things. Once he stopped being bored the world itself seemed to transform completely around him. The best adventures start when you stop being bored.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: Milo returned from the Lands Beyond to find that his bedroom had not changed in any way he could measure. The walls were the same color and the ceiling was the same height and his desk was in the same position. But his experience of the room was so different that it might as well have been a completely new place. He noticed the grain of the wood in his desk and the quality of light coming through the window at this hour. He picked up a dictionary and found himself genuinely curious about words he had previously skipped past. He did a page of arithmetic and found himself noticing patterns he had never bothered to look for before. The adventure had not changed the world — it had changed the boredom that had been preventing him from seeing it. The best adventures start when you stop being bored.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: The Phantom Tollbooth's resolution is more philosophically demanding than most readers initially notice or appreciate. Milo does not return to find that his ordinary world has been secretly magical all along in some hidden literal sense. He returns to find that his ordinary world is genuinely, substantially, and inexhaustibly interesting — which is different. The interest requires something from him — attention, curiosity, the willingness to look carefully and ask real questions. Boredom, Juster suggests, is not a response to a boring world but a refusal to engage with an interesting one. It is a kind of self-protection that costs far more than it saves in terms of what it prevents the bored person from experiencing. When Milo stops being bored he does not need a magical tollbooth because the world he lives in is already the Lands Beyond. The adventure was always available — it was waiting, as all real adventures wait, for someone willing to begin paying attention. The best adventures start when you stop being bored.
